This manuscript demonstrates a mechanochemically driven strategy to reversibly induce and amplify plasmon-coupled circular dichroism (PCCD) within 1D assemblies of achiral gold nanoparticles bridged by bovine serum albumin (BSA). Upon uniaxial macroscopic stretching of the flexible substrate, the entangled interparticle protein bridges undergo conformational reconfiguration and dipole reorientation, yielding an ellipticity of up to 1.18° and a dissymmetry factor ($g$-factor) of ~0.2 with excellent cycling stability (>100 cycles). The underlying mechanism is supported by a comprehensive suite of experiments—including in situ SERS, ATR-FTIR, and enzymatic digestion controls—alongside all-atom molecular dynamics and continuum electromagnetic calculations.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- None. The authors have carried out an exceptionally rigorous and well-controlled study, thoroughly validating the origin of the chiroptical signals and ruling out artifacts such as linear dichroism or purely geometrical plasmonic chirality.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- In the discussion of the SERS selection rules and orientation markers (Fig. 3b,c), please ensure that the normalization procedure for the phenylalanine peak intensity versus total background/substrate response is explicitly stated in the Methods section.
- In Fig. 4c,d, the caption notes scaling factors (0.18 and 0.12) applied to the visual representation of the dipole vectors; it would be helpful to briefly state in the main text or Supplementary Note 3 whether the calculated dipole magnitude scale is linear with strain.
- A few minor typographical details in the main text (e.g., consistent formatting of hyphenation in "molecule–nanostructure" and unit spacing throughout the Methods) should be polished during production.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY: The manuscript demonstrates optical initialization, manipulation, and read-out of nuclear spins in a europium-based molecular complex using optically detected NMR (ODNMR). The authors achieve coherent control via Rabi oscillations, Hahn echoes, and CPMG dynamical decoupling, reporting spin coherence times up to 2 ms. The work represents a significant step toward using molecular nuclear spins for quantum technologies.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- None.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The relationship between the spin hole burning linewidth (T2,s* = 19.3 μs) and the Hahn echo coherence time (T2,s = 0.61 ms) is not fully clarified. The hole width appears to be limited by the RF pulse bandwidth/power, and the authors state that the extracted T2,s* is a lower bound. A brief comment on why the hole burning measurement does not reflect the true homogeneous linewidth (e.g., pulse broadening) would help avoid confusion.
- The spin characterization was performed on a crystal with a broad optical inhomogeneous linewidth (23 GHz) attributed to strain from mounting. Since this is not the best-quality crystal, it would be useful to state explicitly whether the reported spin coherence times are expected to be representative of the intrinsic material or could be improved with strain-free mounting.
- The CPMG scaling exponent β = 0.53 is slightly below the 2/3 expected for a single Lorentzian noise bath. The authors attribute this to a heterogeneous environment; a more detailed discussion of how the different dephasing sources (protons, 13C, paramagnetic impurities, vibrational modes) contribute to the observed scaling would strengthen the interpretation.
- The title uses “coherent spins,” which could be misread as electron spins. Consider “coherently controlled nuclear spins” for precision, though this is a minor wording issue.

DECISION: minor_revision

SUMMARY: This manuscript reports a systematic study of collective emission regimes in films of giant CsPbBr3 perovskite nanocrystals, showing that decreasing temperature and increasing excitation density can drive a transition from amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) to superfluorescence (SF), with standard photoluminescence in between depending on emitter density. The authors combine time-resolved spectroscopy, variable stripe-length measurements, spectral analysis, and numerical simulations to identify distinct signatures of SF and ASE, including a cautionary observation that ASE can mimic SF-like temporal ringing at room temperature.

MAJOR CONCERNS: None.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The abstract states that temperature and excitation density drive transitions between “both regimes” (SF and ASE), but the paper actually discusses three regimes including standard PL. Consider clarifying the phrasing to avoid confusion.
- The distinction between intra-NC (excitons within a single giant nanocrystal) and inter-NC (between different nanocrystals) cooperative effects is acknowledged but could be discussed more explicitly. Since the giant NCs are sub-wavelength and support many excitons, the observed SF may be dominated by intra-NC superradiance rather than collective emission from a multi-NC ensemble. A brief comment on this would strengthen the interpretation.
- The empirical fit model for extracting the SF threshold (Equation 2) is reasonable but somewhat ad hoc. The authors could briefly justify the assumed linear relation between coherently coupled excitons and excitation fluence, or note that this is a phenomenological approximation.
- In the numerical ASE simulation, a constant hot-carrier relaxation time (τh = 5 ps) is assumed. The authors acknowledge that this time can be fluence-dependent in perovskites. A short note on the expected sensitivity of the ringing behavior to variations in τh would be helpful.
- The main text mentions “Burnham–Chiao ringing” as a signature of SF at low temperatures, but this is not shown in any main figure. Since this is an important diagnostic, it would be useful to either display a representative low-temperature time trace with visible ringing or explicitly refer to the supplementary figure where it is presented.
- The FDTD simulation of ASE spectra (Extended Data Fig. 3) shows a redshift of ~65 meV independent of temperature, while the experimental redshift at intermediate temperatures is much smaller. The authors attribute this to SF/ASE coexistence. This is plausible, but a brief sentence clarifying why the spectral redshift would be suppressed in the mixed regime would improve readability.

DECISION: minor_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript reports optical preparation and read-out of nuclear-quadrupole spin populations in a Eu3+-based molecular crystal, together with RF-driven Rabi oscillations, Hahn echoes and CPMG dynamical decoupling. The principal result—optical detection of coherent nuclear-spin control in a molecular complex—is potentially important, with reported Hahn-echo and CPMG coherence times of approximately 0.61 and 2.0 ms, respectively.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The conversion of the spin-hole linewidth into \(T_{2,\mathrm{s}}^*\) is insufficiently explained and appears inconsistent with standard linewidth–coherence relations. A Gaussian hole with FWHM 11.64 kHz does not straightforwardly imply \(T_{2,\mathrm{s}}^*=19.3\) μs; the result depends on the definition of \(T_2^*\), the convolution inherent to hole burning and whether FWHM or HWHM is used. The authors should derive the stated relation explicitly and propagate the linewidth uncertainty. More generally, the optical discussion conflates homogeneous coherence, ensemble \(T_2^*\), instantaneous spectral diffusion and “pure dephasing.” These quantities and symbols should be defined consistently throughout.
- The CPMG analysis is overinterpreted given measurements at only four pulse numbers (\(N=1,2,4,8\)), apparently with one dataset at each point. Fit uncertainties alone do not establish the reproducibility of either the 2-ms coherence time or the exponent \(\beta=0.53(3)\). Moreover, estimating a bath correlation time from a static spin-hole width requires assumptions that are not adequately justified, and the attribution to a heterogeneous bath is not uniquely supported by the observed exponent. Repeated measurements should establish experimental variability; otherwise, the precision should be reduced and the noise-bath interpretation and \(\tau_B\) estimate presented explicitly as model-dependent. There is also an internal inconsistency between describing the Hahn-echo decay as exponential and later stating that all decays, including \(N=1\), were fitted with a stretched exponential of exponent 1.43.
- The manuscript repeatedly refers to optical “initialization” of nuclear-spin states, but the protocol used for the coherent-control experiments burns a single spectral pit and creates a population imbalance rather than preparing the selected ensemble in a uniquely specified hyperfine state. In zero magnetic field, the quadrupolar \(|m_I|\) levels also retain degeneracies. The operational state preparation and read-out should be described precisely, and implications for a controllable qubit should distinguish ensemble coherence from initialization and read-out of a non-degenerate two-level system.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The best optical linewidth is obtained from a 1.94-GHz crystal, whereas spin characterization is performed on a different crystal with a 23-GHz optical linewidth. This distinction should be made prominent in the main figures and conclusions so that properties from separate specimens are not inadvertently presented as one combined material benchmark.
- Given the use of RF powers up to approximately 92 W in liquid helium, the authors should report coil calibration, RF duty cycle and checks for sample heating, particularly for the CPMG sequences.
- Clarify whether quoted uncertainties are standard errors, confidence intervals or fit covariance estimates, and provide residuals or goodness-of-fit measures for the principal coherence fits.
- Temper statements that coherence will improve at millikelvin temperatures or with more decoupling pulses; these are plausible expectations rather than demonstrated conclusions.
- Correct minor wording and typographical issues, including “more than a factor of three,” “a factor of three,” “narrow spin inhomogeneous lines,” and the decimal comma in “11,64 kHz.”

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript reports excitation-density- and temperature-dependent emission from dilute and dense films of giant CsPbBr3 nanocrystals, assigning low-temperature accelerated emission to superfluorescence and high-temperature emission in dense films to amplified spontaneous emission. Variable-stripe-length measurements and Maxwell–Bloch-type simulations are used to support the ASE assignment and to show that ASE can generate ringing resembling a conventional superfluorescence signature.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The evidence for superfluorescence remains insufficiently discriminating. The central assignment rests on fluence-dependent lifetime shortening, superlinear peak intensity, build-up dynamics and ringing, yet the manuscript itself demonstrates that several of these signatures can arise from ASE. Moreover, multiexciton radiative recombination, Auger dynamics, carrier cooling and stimulated emission are plausible at the reported occupancies (approximately 44 excitons per nanocrystal per 1 µJ cm−2). Equation 2 is an empirical threshold function rather than a fit to a superfluorescence model and therefore cannot establish the mechanism. The authors should quantitatively test established SF scaling relations for the delay time, pulse duration and cooperative number, and provide an observable more directly connected to macroscopic polarization—such as first-order coherence, photon correlations, single-shot delay statistics, or an equivalent measurement. At minimum, competing multiexciton and stimulated-emission models must be fitted and excluded quantitatively.
- ASE has not been adequately excluded in the nominally low-density, low-temperature samples. The principal measurements use a roughly 200-µm pump spot, which provides a substantial propagation distance, while the small-spot experiment is presented only for the dense sample at room temperature. Variable-stripe-length or pump-size-dependent measurements should be performed on the dilute sample in the claimed SF regime, together with an experimental upper bound on its modal gain. Quantitative film thicknesses, nanocrystal volume fractions/densities, optical constants, propagation losses and supported waveguide modes are also needed; “low density” and “high density” are presently preparation labels rather than measured parameters.
- The dephasing argument underlying the proposed regime boundary is qualitative and relies on T2 values inferred from smaller nanocrystals and even a different halide composition. The measured ensemble linewidth at 6 K is 12 meV and cannot by itself support the asserted long coherence time or distinguish homogeneous from inhomogeneous broadening. The authors should measure T2 for these giant nanocrystals, or clearly delimit the conclusions and demonstrate quantitatively that measured τD and τR satisfy the appropriate SF criterion over the assigned regime. The condition printed as \(T_2>\tau_D\tau_R\) is dimensionally inconsistent; if \(T_2>\sqrt{\tau_D\tau_R}\) is intended, this must be corrected throughout and used consistently in the analysis.
- The room-temperature ringing simulations are qualitative and contain adjustable or phenomenological ingredients, including the spontaneous-emission source, β, a fixed hot-carrier relaxation time and assumed excited fractions that are not mapped to measured fluences. They show that the proposed mechanism is possible, but do not establish that it uniquely explains the experiment. The statement that the dynamics can be “explained only with ASE” should be removed unless supported by quantitative agreement, parameter sensitivity analysis and exclusion of alternatives.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The claim that \(V<\lambda^3\) places excitons within an individual nanocrystal in the Dicke regime is too strong. This geometric condition is not sufficient without demonstrating spectral indistinguishability, appropriate spatial phase and coherence among the excitons.
- The assertion that linear time-integrated emission excludes non-radiative quenching is not generally valid, particularly for highly multiexcitonic populations. Fluence-dependent quantum yield or an explicit rate-equation analysis would be more informative.
- The dismissal of biexciton, plasma or bandgap-renormalization contributions to the redshifted peak solely by comparison with reported binding energies is incomplete, especially far above the Mott density. The ASE assignment should also discuss excitation-induced spectral shifts and many-body effects.
- The abstract should temper “demonstrate the transition” and “excitonic SF was observed” unless the mechanistic concerns above are resolved. The suggested quantum-light-source application is also not supported by photon-statistics measurements.
- Several presentation errors should be corrected, including “AbstractInteractions”, duplicated “Quantum optics” subject terms, missing spaces and malformed equations. Reference 12 lacks a proper first-author name, and the data DOI cited in the Data Availability section differs from that in reference 48.
- The manuscript should distinguish clearly between normal-direction and edge-collected measurements in every relevant figure caption.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript reports that mechanical stretching of bovine serum albumin (BSA) molecules anchored within achiral gold nanoparticle chains strongly enhances and reversibly modulates plasmon-coupled circular dichroism (PCCD), achieving ellipticity of 1.18° and a dissymmetry factor of 0.2, with >100 switching cycles. The authors attribute this effect to strain-induced conformational changes in BSA (partial recovery of α-helices and reorientation of molecular dipoles) that overcome the concurrent weakening of plasmonic hotspots, supported by MD simulations, electromagnetic modeling, SERS, and ATR-FTIR. The work establishes a new route to dynamically tunable chiroptical activity in achiral plasmonic assemblies.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
None. The authors have convincingly addressed the key mechanistic and control experiments (rotation tests, CTAC controls, NP size dependence, enzymatic digestion, pH-induced disentanglement) that validate the origin and reversibility of the PCCD signal. The combination of experimental spectroscopy, protein simulations, and electromagnetic modeling provides a coherent and compelling explanation for the counterintuitive increase in PCCD upon stretching, despite the enlargement of interparticle gaps.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The sentence in the main text "analysing all the CD spectra presented a contribution of CD scattering must also be considered" is grammatically awkward and could be rephrased for clarity.
- The statement "Both CD amplitudes and g-factor increased by 10 and 1,000 times, respectively, compared with previously reported PCCD values" would benefit from explicitly citing the baseline values from Extended Data Table 1 in the text, to avoid ambiguity.
- The description of the pH-switching experiment is somewhat lengthy; a more concise summary in the main text, with details moved to Supplementary, might improve readability.
- Minor typographical errors and capitalization inconsistencies (e.g., "Proteinase K" vs. "proteinase K") should be corrected.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY: The authors show that fibrillar adhesions (FBs), through anchoring of the vimentin intermediate filament network via plectin 1f, maintain nuclear deformation and nuclear localization of mechano-sensitive factors (YAP, twist, snail, and a nucleocytoplasmic transport reporter) after loss of actomyosin contractility or upon substrate softening. FB–vimentin coupling thereby sets the timescale of mechano-adaptation (~1 h, matching FB disassembly kinetics) and shields the nucleus from stretch-induced deformation and DNA damage, supported by a finite-element model. The revision has addressed prior concerns substantially, with multiple independent FB-inhibition approaches, cell-type controls, photodegradable hydrogels, and a documented computational model.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- None that require further experimentation. The pharmacological dissociation of FB loss from general actin disruption (cytoD vs latA) is now well supported by the basal actin, SMIFH2, and micropatterning data, and the vimentin/plectin 1f-8/nesprin-3 perturbations adequately establish the mechanistic link. The model is appropriately framed as qualitative, with sensitivity analysis and code availability.

MINOR CONCERNS:
1. The claim that FBs act as a "low-pass filter" is appealing but the manuscript only demonstrates the filter on the *loss* of stimulation (contractility inhibition, gel softening, Mn²⁺ washout). A brief tempering of the low-pass-filter language, or a direct test of the response to an acute increase in force, would strengthen the analogy.
2. The correlation between FB area and YAP N/C ratio (R² ≈ 0.80; Fig. 1g) pools different drugs and time points; the authors should clarify that this is a population-level correlation across conditions, not a within-condition predictive relationship, to avoid over-interpretation.
3. The mechanism connecting plectin 1f to FBs remains unidentified (acknowledged in the Outlook). It would help to state more explicitly in the results (not only the Outlook) that the plectin 1f–FB interaction is inferred from localization and dominant-negative data rather than directly demonstrated biochemically.
4. Nuclear height measurements rely on lamin B staining and peak-to-peak intensity profiles; a comment on measurement error/precision and whether nuclear volume (not just height) changes would be useful.
5. In the stretch experiments, the model assumes frictional FB–substrate slip bonds; the experimental evidence for the frictional (rather than elastic) nature of this coupling is indirect. This assumption should be flagged as such in the main text.
6. Minor: several Extended Data figures have small n and only 2 independent replicates (e.g., ED Fig. 5g,h western blots, ED Fig. 8); ensure the text does not over-rely on these. Also correct typographical inconsistencies ("gluteraldehyde" → "glutaraldehyde"; "Snaka51" vs "SNAKA51"; "mages" in ED Fig. 5 caption).
7. The Sencyt t0.5 analysis (Fig. 4m) should state how the 50% threshold time was defined for cells that do not reach 50% within the acquisition window, if any.

DECISION: minor_revision

SUMMARY:
This manuscript demonstrates that fibrillar adhesions (FBs) maintain the nucleus in a flattened, mechanically deformed state following the loss of actomyosin contractility by anchoring the vimentin intermediate filament network through plectin 1f. This structural coupling effectively acts as a low-pass mechanical filter, dictating that nuclear shape changes and downstream mechanotransduction (such as YAP, Snail, and Twist nucleocytoplasmic shuttling) occur on the slower timescale of FB disassembly (~1 hour) rather than rapid focal adhesion or contractility turnover. Furthermore, the authors combine molecular perturbations, in situ photodegradable hydrogels, stretch assays, and continuum computational modeling to show that this vimentin–FB link dissipates external mechanical stress and protects the genome against stretch-induced DNA damage.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- None.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- Please ensure consistent spelling of "glutaraldehyde" throughout the text and Extended Data figure legends (e.g., "gluteraldehyde" appears in several Extended Data figure captions and headings).
- In the discussion of the computational model, briefly clarify in the main text that the nucleus is treated as a linear elastic material, acknowledging that while viscous relaxation could modulate transient deformation magnitudes, it does not alter the steady-state mechanical anchoring conclusions.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY:
The manuscript presents a multi-scale computational framework that integrates machine-learned atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials, Onsager multicomponent transport theory, and cellular automaton kinetics (ReactCA) to predict solid-state reaction pathways and phase selectivity. Applied to the polymorph-rich Ba–Ti–O system, the authors demonstrate that cross-ion correlations and diffusion kinetics through disordered/liquid-like interphases govern intermediate phase selection across varying temperatures and stoichiometries, resolving long-standing discrepancies between purely thermodynamic models and experimental observations.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- None.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- In the Methods section under "Accelerating AIMD using ACE" (second paragraph), there appears to be a typo in the listed stoichiometry: "Ba6Ti27O40" should presumably read "Ba6Ti17O40" to be consistent with the main text and phase diagrams.
- In the Methods section under "Simulation of solid-state synthesis reactions with ReactCA", ensure consistent spacing in the section header (currently written as "ReactCAA") and consistent mathematical formatting for the scoring function definitions.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY: The manuscript argues that fibrillar adhesions prolong nuclear mechanical deformation and mechanosensitive transcription-factor localization after loss of contractility by anchoring the vimentin network to fibronectin through plectin 1f. Photodegradable substrates, mechanical stretching and computational modelling further suggest that this coupling delays adaptation to substrate softening and protects nuclei from acute deformation and damage.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The statistical treatment does not consistently account for the hierarchical structure of the data. In many comparisons, tens to hundreds of cells or adhesions pooled across only two to five independent experiments are treated as independent observations in Mann–Whitney tests, t-tests or ANOVA. This is particularly problematic for adhesion-level measurements, where multiple adhesions are sampled from the same cell. The principal conclusions should be reanalysed using biological replicate as the experimental unit or mixed-effects models with experiment and, where relevant, cell as nested random effects. Effect sizes and confidence intervals should also be reported.
- The evidence that fibrillar-adhesion remodelling itself “sets” the approximately 1-h adaptation timescale remains partly correlative. Adhesion lifetimes are measured during spontaneous turnover on glass or static polyacrylamide substrates, rather than directly during photochemical softening, and the measured decay is then imposed on the model. Direct tracking of tensin-positive adhesions and Sencyt/nuclear shape in the same softening experiment would substantially strengthen the causal connection. Alternatively, the manuscript should moderate the claim to state that fibrillar-adhesion persistence is consistent with, and contributes to, the observed adaptation timescale.
- Relatedly, the term “low-pass filter” and the claim that the mechanism regulates responses to both increased and decreased mechanical stimulation are stronger than the experiments establish. The study primarily examines step decreases in contractility or stiffness; the stretch experiments assess shielding from a single acute load rather than frequency-dependent mechanotransduction. Demonstrating filtering would require controlled oscillatory inputs over multiple frequencies, or the terminology should be revised to “mechanical persistence”, “delayed adaptation” or an equivalent formulation.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- Clarify throughout that the proposed plectin 1f linkage is inferred from localization and dominant-negative perturbation; the direct molecular binding partner within fibrillar adhesions remains unknown.
- The model contains fitted or assumed adhesion forces and friction parameters and uses a linear-elastic nucleus without intrinsic viscoelastic relaxation. These limitations are acknowledged in Methods but should be stated more prominently when quantitative agreement with experiment is discussed.
- Several conclusions are presented as broadly applicable to “cells” or intermediate filaments generally, although most mechanistic experiments use one immortalized fibroblast line. The scope should be qualified accordingly.
- Correct typographical and formatting issues, including “AbstractAbstract”, “GPF” instead of “GFP” in Fig. 3, “gluteraldehyde” instead of “glutaraldehyde”, “cell’s ability”, and malformed equation formatting in the N/C-ratio and modelling sections.
- Report exact P values where feasible rather than only thresholded significance, and distinguish clearly between numbers of cells, adhesions, biological replicates and technical replicates in every caption.
- The description of adhesion disassembly as a Gaussian fit requires justification. Adhesion intensity trajectories are not generally expected to be Gaussian, and censoring or exclusion of adhesions not fully formed and lost within the imaging window should be described.

DECISION: major_revision

**SUMMARY:** The authors integrate machine-learned interatomic potential-derived Onsager transport coefficients for liquid-like interphase analogues of candidate products into the ReactCA cellular automaton framework, and apply this to Ba–Ti–O solid-state synthesis from BaO/TiO2 precursors. They show that including cross-ion correlations and diffusive fluxes reproduces experimentally observed phase evolution (products, intermediates, impurities) across four precursor stoichiometries and temperature/time profiles, whereas thermodynamics-only scoring does not, and they interpret the selectivity in terms of Ba–Ba/Ti–Ti ion correlations tied to local coordination environments.

**MAJOR CONCERNS:**

- **Validation of the ACE potential for transport, not just energies/forces.** The potential is benchmarked (Supplementary Section 3) on energies and forces, but the quantity actually used is the Green–Kubo time-correlation function slope. Transport coefficients are notoriously sensitive to subtle potential errors and to finite trajectory length; 5-ns trajectories with a 200-ps fit window for a viscous melt may not be converged, especially at 750–1,000 K where dynamics are slow. The authors should demonstrate convergence of L_ij with trajectory length and number of replicates, and report uncertainty propagation into K_D and ultimately into the simulated phase fractions. The stated error bars (std. dev. over five trajectories) likely underestimate systematic error.

- **Circularity/parameter sensitivity in the scoring function.** The scoring function contains several fitted constants (a, b, c, d, e, s = 5×10^13) carried over from ref. 19, with s chosen "to ensure the reaction between the precursors initiate at temperatures above the decomposition temperature of BaCO3." This is effectively tuning to the known answer for the one test system presented. The authors should demonstrate that conclusions are robust to reasonable variation of these parameters, or justify that they are transferable and not refit for Ba–Ti–O.

- **Single-system demonstration.** All quantitative validation is in one chemical space (Ba–Ti–O) with one precursor pair. Given the strong claims of generality ("a general, predictive framework"), the authors should either (i) temper the generality claim, or (ii) show at least one additional chemical system—ideally one with variable oxidation states excluded by the current approximation—to demonstrate transferability. At minimum, the limitations (single oxidation state, μ̃ ≈ μ approximation, core–shell geometry, uniform particle size) should be consolidated and discussed more prominently as constraints on applicability.

- **The "liquid-like interphase" hypothesis is assumed, not tested.** The central physical assumption—that transport occurs through an amorphous layer with the stoichiometry of the nucleating crystalline product—is plausible but not directly evidenced. Is there experimental or simulation evidence for such layers, their thickness, and their composition? The chemical potential gradient is approximated using a fixed layer thickness h (Supplementary Fig. 8); sensitivity of K_D to h should be reported, since K_D scales inversely with it and this directly feeds the scoring function.

- **Quantitative comparison with experiments is loose.** Agreement is repeatedly described as "excellent" or "qualitative," but comparisons are largely narrative (e.g., reconciling ref. 22 by asserting "their experiment maps onto the early stages of our simulation"). The authors should provide quantitative metrics (phase fraction errors, time/temperature of phase onsets) and include a fair uncertainty band on the experimental side. The post hoc rationalization for reaction 2 weakens the predictive claim.

**MINOR CONCERNS:**

- Abstract typo: "AbstractEstablishing..." (formatting error).
- Fig. 2a caption says hull computed "at 600 °C" while text discusses 1,000–1,750 K; clarify the temperature range over which the hull shape is claimed invariant and show the evidence.
- Equation numbering/equation 8 appears mis-set ("81−(1−y)^1/3=2KD t/r0"); check typesetting.
- The claim that Ba2TiO4 formation "cannot be explained" by the nucleation-barrier metric (ref. 35) deserves a brief physical explanation, not just the observation.
- Reference 22 year/page ("58, 454–54") appears garbled.
- In the Discussion, the sentence "we included the nucleation rate computed using the approach in ref. 35" is missing a period and reads awkwardly.
- It would help the reader to state early on which phases are included/excluded (e.g., Ba3TiO5 is shown red in Fig. 2a but its exclusion rationale is not given in the main text).
- The Tammann-temperature treatment ("non-zero, but only slightly positive" scores below Tammann) should be justified—why should reactions proceed at all below the empirical threshold?
- Consider reporting the fitted Onsager matrix elements themselves (not only K_D) in the main or supplementary data for reproducibility; Supplementary Data 1 reference should be cross-checked (it cites Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9 for transport coefficients, but Fig. 8 in the main text is the ReactCA schematic—likely supplementary figure numbering confusion).

**DECISION:** minor_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript presents a granular composite biomaterial ("MAGIC matrix") that combines alginate microgels with a Matrigel interstitium, enabling both embedded bioprinting of dense cell slurries and support of complex organoid self-organization. The authors identify stress relaxation at long timescales and large strains as a key rheological determinant of morphogenesis, and demonstrate that bioprinting into MAGIC matrix improves organoid reproducibility and assay statistical power across multiple tissue types.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The causal link between stress relaxation and morphogenesis is inferred from comparisons of two MAGIC matrix compositions (1:1 and 2:1 AMG:Matrigel) that have matched linear viscoelastic moduli but differ in stress relaxation. While this is a clever design, it does not rule out other microstructural differences (e.g., pore size, interstitial ligand density, or local packing) that could independently influence organoid development. The authors should either provide a more direct manipulation of stress relaxation (e.g., varying interstitial viscosity while keeping microgel fraction constant) or explicitly acknowledge this limitation and temper the claim that stress relaxation is "required" for optimal morphogenesis, replacing it with "important" or "critical".
- The bioprinting platform is described in detail, but its advantages over existing embedded printing methods (e.g., pneumatic extrusion, as in Brassard et al. 2021) are not quantitatively benchmarked. A head-to-head comparison of printing resolution, cell viability post-printing, and throughput would strengthen the claims of technological advancement.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- In Fig. 2m, only the average relaxation time from the stretched exponential fit is reported; the stretching exponent (β) would provide additional insight into the relaxation spectrum and should be included.
- The statement "orders-of-magnitude improvement in statistical power" is somewhat misleading: the power analysis shows an ~8-fold reduction in required sample size (n=12 vs n=100), while the p-value improvement at fixed n is indeed orders of magnitude. The phrasing should be clarified to distinguish between these two metrics.
- The manuscript is very long and dense, and some methodological details (e.g., exact printhead calibration procedures) are only in the Supplementary Information. While acceptable, a brief summary of key parameters in the main text would improve readability.

DECISION: minor_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript reports that uniaxial stretching of BSA-functionalized, nominally achiral gold nanoparticle chains increases their visible–near-infrared circular dichroism by approximately 22-fold, reaching an ellipticity of 1.18° and a reported dissymmetry factor of 0.2, with reversible modulation over 100 cycles. The authors attribute this unusually large response to mechanically induced recovery and alignment of protein secondary structure within interparticle gaps, supported by spectroscopy, molecular dynamics and electromagnetic modelling.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The exceptionally large claimed PCCD response still requires more rigorous exclusion of polarization artefacts. These samples combine strongly aligned nanoparticle chains, strained birefringent PDMS, an anisotropic PEI layer and substantial scattering; conventional CD spectroscopy and ellipsometric extraction can therefore mix circular dichroism with linear dichroism, linear birefringence, depolarization and differential scattering. Sample rotation alone does not adequately exclude these effects. Full Mueller-matrix measurements under strain should be provided, including all relevant linear terms and depolarization, azimuthal dependence, front/back illumination, and raw LCP/RCP transmission or extinction. Strained bare PDMS/PEI and achiral-ligand controls should be matched as closely as possible in chain morphology, extinction and interparticle-gap evolution. Because the manuscript acknowledges a circular-differential-scattering contribution, absorption and scattering should be separated, for example by integrating-sphere measurements, before the signal is assigned quantitatively to molecule-induced plasmonic CD.
- The reported \(g=0.2\), central to the significance claim, is insufficiently defined and validated for a strongly scattering film. The precise equation, extinction/absorbance denominator, baseline corrections, spectral uncertainties and consistency between ellipsometry and conventional CD must be reported. Independent sample preparations and confidence intervals are needed for the peak ellipticity, \(g\)-factor, enhancement ratio and cycling performance; measurements at positions on one substrate or repeated cycles on one device are not independent replicates.
- The evidence does not yet conclusively establish that protein stretching and secondary-structure recovery cause the enhancement. A BSA molecule is described as covalently attached to only one particle, so tensile-force transmission across widening gaps relies on poorly characterized adsorption or intermolecular entanglement. The experiments do not directly measure protein extension, load-bearing contacts, or dipole orientation. The SERS changes are strongly confounded by the rapidly changing hotspot enhancement, while the small amide-I shift from approximately 1,660 to 1,655 cm\(^{-1}\) is not by itself specific evidence for α-helix recovery; quantitative band analysis, strain-matched controls and replicate measurements are required. Polarized vibrational spectroscopy or another direct orientation-sensitive measurement would substantially strengthen the proposed mechanism.
- The MD simulations are too idealized and strongly driven to serve as mechanistic validation in their present form. A curved nanoparticle gap is replaced by planar walls; water is removed; one covalent attachment is imposed; and a force of 100 kcal mol\(^{-1}\) Å\(^{-1}\) is applied to every atom of the mobile gold wall, without mapping this loading protocol to experimental force, time or strain. The authors should report force–extension behaviour, protein–wall contacts, anchoring stability, replicate trajectories and sensitivity to hydration, loading rate and initial orientation. The predicted refolding during separation under dry conditions also requires physical justification.
- Structural or extrinsic chirality of the strained assemblies has not been excluded at the level warranted by a \(g\)-factor comparable to intentionally chiral plasmonic structures. Chain fragmentation, lateral particle offsets, partial embedding and substrate asymmetry can produce three-dimensional or extrinsic chiral configurations not captured by top-view AFM. Quantitative structural statistics before and during stretching, including out-of-plane information, should be supplied and incorporated into electromagnetic controls without a chiral molecular constitutive parameter. The statement that an “anti-Cotton” line shape directly distinguishes PCCD from structural CD is not generally valid and should not be used as proof of origin.
- The COMSOL model appears primarily phenomenological: it prescribes a chiral continuous medium and mixtures of “stretched” and “non-stretched” states, then reproduces spectral tendencies. The manuscript should explain how the chirality tensor and mixture parameters are independently obtained from the MD or spectroscopy, whether the absolute CD magnitude and \(g\)-factor are predicted without fitting, and whether gap enlargement, oligomer fragmentation and substrate effects are included. Otherwise, the modelling cannot substantiate the claimed molecular mechanism or distinguish it from alternative origins.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The manuscript demonstrates reversible modulation of CD magnitude, not reversal of handedness or CD sign. Statements such as “dynamic reversal of chirality” should be replaced by “reversible switching/modulation” unless sign reversal is experimentally shown.
- The title’s phrase “between protein and achiral plasmonic assemblies” could imply bidirectional transfer; “from protein to…” would more accurately describe the experiments.
- Claims including “all [BSA molecules] contribute to PCCD,” “pure PCCD,” “conclusively validates,” and “redefining the efficiency limits” are stronger than supported and should be moderated.
- The pH experiment has several simultaneous variables—protein conformation, adsorption, aggregation, hydration history, particle spacing and local refractive index—and therefore should not be presented as conclusive validation of entanglement.
- Proteinase K digestion supports a role for BSA but does not alone distinguish molecular PCCD from BSA-dependent structural rearrangement. Quantitative morphology, extinction and particle-spacing comparisons before and after digestion should accompany this control.
- The anchoring discussion should distinguish evidence that Cys34 is the principal available thiol from proof that every BSA molecule adopts a single Cys34-mediated attachment geometry in this assembly.
- The claimed “self-healing” after overnight water immersion should be defined structurally and tested over repeated healing cycles.
- Several textual and production issues require correction, including “AbstractAbstract,” merged sentences, “dg,h,” “serume albumin,” “table the Universitat,” inconsistent strain values for proteolysis (approximately 50% in the main text versus 40% in Methods), and incomplete/duplicated supplementary-information listings.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY:
This manuscript introduces a high-throughput, all-optical method combining interferometric scattering (iSCAT) microscopy and photoluminescence (PL) imaging to simultaneously determine the physical dimensions and single-particle photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of thousands of individual colloidal CsPbBr3 nanocrystals in situ. Applying this approach across the lifecycle of the nanocrystals, the authors reveal an intrinsic size–PLQY anticorrelation governed by halide-vacancy defects, uncover size-dependent kinetics during post-synthetic chemical defect repair, and resolve the real-time dynamics of photoinduced degradation, showing that degradation halts due to electron trapping by photogenerated metallic lead (Pb0).

MAJOR CONCERNS:
None. The revised manuscript is thorough, rigorously validated against ensemble standards (TEM sizing, integrating sphere, and chemical actinometry), and provides deep mechanistic insights that resolve longstanding questions in perovskite nanocrystal photophysics.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- In the main text (first paragraph under "Determining perovskite nanocrystal size simultaneous to emission"), the volume range is written as "1.000–13.800 nm³", where periods are used instead of commas/no separators, which could be misread as decimals rather than thousands (1,000–13,800 nm³).
- In the Methods section under "Sample preparation for XPS and SEM measurements", the laser power density is listed as "110 kW m⁻²", whereas in the main text and optical setup section, power densities are reported in "kW cm⁻²" (e.g., 100–240 kW cm⁻²). Please ensure unit consistency across the text and methods.
- In equation definitions in the Methods (e.g., polarizability α), a few duplicate symbols and spacing issues appear from the LaTeX-to-text rendering (e.g., "αα", "νν"); please ensure final typesetting is cleanly formatted.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY: The authors present a combined iSCAT/photoluminescence microscopy approach that determines the size and PLQY of thousands of individual CsPbBr3 nanocubes in solution, calibrated against TEM. Applied across the nanocrystal "life cycle", the method reveals a size–PLQY anticorrelation in pristine samples, size-dependent enhancement kinetics during PbBr2/ligand defect repair (attributed to halide vacancies), and power-dependent photoinduced degradation halted by Pb0 formation.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The iSCAT contrast-to-volume calibration relies on matching percentiles of an iSCAT distribution to percentiles of a TEM distribution of "the same sample" (Fig. 1c). This is a distribution-level, not particle-level, calibration. Any systematic difference between the two measurement populations (e.g., selection bias in TEM sampling, particle loss during grid preparation, aggregation) propagates directly into all absolute size, cross-section and PLQY values. The authors should justify why percentile matching is valid and provide an uncertainty estimate on the conversion factor beyond the fit confidence band; ideally, a small set of individually correlated particles (e.g., via AFM or correlated TEM of the same particles) would strengthen the calibration.
- The absorption cross-section is computed from a quasistatic sphere polarizability model with a uniform dielectric function. The authors acknowledge this, but the claimed ~10.4% statistical error does not obviously include systematic errors from the shape/sphere approximation, the choice of dielectric function (which for CsPbBr3 varies substantially between literature sources), or the unknown refractive index of the degraded Pb0-containing remnant. Please provide a full error budget, including how the η correction factor (which folds in "variations relative to a reference bulk measurement") is determined and whether it risks circularity in benchmarking against ensemble PLQY.
- The size–PLQY anticorrelation is a central claim. Since PLQY is derived from the iSCAT-derived size, any size-dependent bias in the iSCAT contrast (e.g., contrast nonlinearity with volume, particle–surface proximity effects, contrast contributions from ligand shell) could partially generate this anticorrelation artefactually. The authors should demonstrate that the anticorrelation survives alternative calibration assumptions or independent size estimates for a subset of particles.
- The degradation mechanism (Pb0 trapping photoinduced electrons halting material loss) is plausible but rests on indirect evidence: XPS on a separate ensemble sample, SEM size distributions, and correlation of PL and iSCAT signal loss. The alternative that the residual iSCAT signal arises from a changed refractive index rather than size reduction is addressed by SEM, but only ensemble-level. The authors should discuss (and ideally test) whether Pb0 could itself contribute to the residual iSCAT contrast, and temper the causal language accordingly.
- Samples are from a single synthesis batch, and measurements span weeks during which the bulk QY aged from 26% to 44%. This aging is a significant confounder for the in situ enhancement experiments (Fig. 3): some of the observed PLQY changes could reflect time-dependent aging rather than the added species. The OAm-only and component-isolation controls help, but the authors should quantify aging drift under identical measurement conditions without additions.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- Fig. 1c: fitting TEM volume vs iSCAT contrast with a linear model forced through the origin should be justified; the fit residuals and whether a non-zero intercept is physically expected (e.g., ligand shell contribution) merit discussion.
- The claim "smaller nanocubes are surprisingly associated with higher PLQY" — the word "surprisingly" is subjective; consider removing or citing prior observations of size-dependent QY in perovskite nanocrystals.
- PCA (Fig. 3b) is used descriptively; loading vectors from only two conditions should be interpreted cautiously.
- The XPS illumination power density is given as "110 kW m−2" in Methods but "kW cm−2" elsewhere — please check units for consistency.
- Typos: "a the illumination source", "JOEL" (JEOL), "FijiJ" (Fiji).
- The manuscript would benefit from stating explicitly how many independent batches/replicates support each key conclusion.

DECISION: minor_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript proposes a multiscale framework that combines machine-learning molecular dynamics, Onsager transport coefficients and thermodynamic reaction energies within the ReactCA cellular automaton to predict phase evolution in Ba–Ti–O solid-state synthesis. The authors report qualitative agreement with several literature syntheses and argue that correlated ionic transport through composition-matched, liquid-like interphases explains kinetic phase selectivity beyond thermodynamics alone.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The manuscript continues to claim prediction “as a function of time”, but the relation between ReactCA steps and physical time is not established. The scoring function contains an empirical scale factor \(s=5\times10^{13}\), selected so that reactions initiate above the BaCO3 decomposition temperature, while particle size is fixed at 0.1 µm irrespective of the experiments being compared. Without an independently determined mapping to seconds, or validation against measured conversion-versus-time data, comparisons involving annealing duration and statements about early versus late stages are qualitative post hoc assignments rather than time-resolved predictions. The authors should either provide and validate a physical time calibration, including particle-size dependence, or substantially narrow the claims throughout.
- The conversion of the Onsager matrix into the scalar \(K_D\) requires stronger physical justification. Growth of a stoichiometric phase is normally constrained by the limiting constituent flux and interfacial mass balance, whereas equation (7) sums contributions from all \(i,j\), divided by \(n_i^\gamma\), such that excess flux of one species may apparently increase the growth rate despite insufficient flux of another. It is also unclear how oxygen flux, electroneutrality, the chosen centre-of-mass frame and potentially negative cross terms are handled in producing a non-negative reaction rate. A complete derivation and tests against explicit limiting-flux alternatives are needed, especially because the central claim concerns the importance of cross-ion coefficients.
- The assumed “liquid-like” interphase having exactly the stoichiometry of each candidate crystalline product remains an unvalidated modelling hypothesis. Agreement with selected literature phase sequences does not by itself establish that such interphases occur, particularly because interfacial disorder, composition gradients, defects and precursor-dependent structures could yield very different transport. At minimum, the authors should provide sensitivity tests to interphase density, disorder preparation, composition and particle size, and clearly distinguish evidence for this physical mechanism from evidence that the resulting effective descriptor improves ReactCA predictions.
- There is an apparent contradiction in the finite-temperature thermodynamics. The Fig. 2 caption states that the phases and relative formation energies defining the hull remain unchanged over all temperatures considered, whereas the Discussion states that Ba2Ti9O20 becomes thermodynamically stable only above 1,373 K and invokes temperature-dependent equilibrium assemblages. The manuscript must reconcile these statements and show the relevant finite-temperature convex hulls or phase equilibria used by ReactCA. Otherwise, it is difficult to determine whether the reported high-temperature selectivity arises from thermodynamics, transport or the heuristic scoring function.
- The validation needs a more systematic uncertainty and ablation analysis. The experimental comparisons are presently narrative and combine studies with incompletely specified times, precursor sizes and processing histories; one comparison is explicitly assigned to an unspecified “early stage” of the simulation. Moreover, the title and conclusions emphasize ion correlations, yet the self-diffusion-only calculations are said to remain qualitatively similar, with the principal evidence relegated to Supplementary Fig. 1. Phase-fraction errors, stochastic ReactCA variability, uncertainty propagated from ACE/Onsager calculations and quantitative comparisons among thermodynamics-only, self-only and full-Onsager models should be reported. This is necessary to support the assertion that cross-ion transport is “critical”, rather than a modest refinement.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The active-learning composition list appears to contain serious nomenclature or transcription errors: Ba6Ti27O40 and BaTi2O2 are listed, whereas the main text discusses Ba6Ti17O40 and other different phases. The complete set of nine candidate products and all training compositions should be checked and stated consistently.
- The manuscript should specify whether any parameters in the scoring function, beyond the stated scale factor, were adjusted after examining the four experimental datasets. A clear separation between calibration and validation data is needed.
- The phrase “rigorously computed ionic diffusion coefficients” is too strong given the machine-learned potential, amorphous-state construction and chemical-potential approximations. “Atomistically estimated transport coefficients” would be more accurate.
- The interpretation of negative Ba–Ba distinct correlations as “mutual repulsion under a chemical potential gradient” is overly direct. A negative distinct contribution denotes anticorrelated collective displacement and does not, by itself, establish a repulsive interaction.
- Please report convergence of the Onsager coefficients with trajectory length and system size, particularly at 750–1,000 K, where an amorphous configuration may be non-ergodic over 5 ns.
- The manuscript alternates between “Tammann” and “Tamman”; the former should be used consistently.
- Numerous production errors require correction, including “AbstractEstablishing”, “MainThe”, “interphasial”, the malformed equation numbering around equation (8), missing spaces between formulas and prose, and inconsistent capitalization/formulas in the references.
- Claims of “excellent” or “accurate” agreement should be moderated unless supported by quantitative goodness-of-fit measures.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript reports a cryo-EM structure of an 8 MDa Hdr–Vhu–Fwd electron-bifurcating super-assembly from the class I methanogen *Methanococcus maripaludis*, comprising 252 subunits organized as two hexameric Hdr–Vhu rings bridged by tetrameric Fwd cores via VhuB polyferredoxins. The authors support the in vivo relevance with cryo-ET of intact cells, probe electron flow by in situ FTIR, identify a modular exchange of the hydrogenase input module with formate dehydrogenase, and argue that this architecture is specific to class I methanogens, contrasting with the class II Hdr–Fmd assembly.

MAJOR CONCERNS:

1. **Quantitative metal/cofactor analysis is described in Methods but not reported.** The ICP-MS section is thorough, yet no metal-stoichiometry data appear in the text, figures, or tables. Given the claim of "over 600 redox cofactors" and the unusual non-cubane clusters, Cys–Sec relay feature, and tungsten incorporation, experimental validation of metal content (Fe, Ni, W, Se) against the model is essential. This was presumably addressed in the first round; if not, it must be.

2. **The Cys–Sec redox relay is speculative and needs clearer demarcation.** The "continuous feature" between A3 and FAD, interpreted as a selenylsulfide bridge, is at ~33 Å from FAD and its chemical identity is unresolved. The authors appropriately hedge, but at Nature level this interpretation should be explicitly labelled as a hypothesis and tempered in the abstract/discussion; presently the text reads more assertively than the evidence warrants. What is the density for the proposed Cys–Sec pair at 3.04 Å—could an ordered water, small ligand, or metal ion fit instead?

3. **Evidence for functional coupling is indirect.** The FTIR experiments are elegant, but the conclusion that CO₂-to-formate conversion occurs "through FdhAB" rests on a decrease of the 2,338 cm⁻¹ CO₂ band. Since the purified preparation contains both Fwd and FdhAB, the experiment does not distinguish which enzyme reduces CO₂, and no product (formate) is detected. Complementary assays (e.g., formate quantification, activity measurements with/without heterodisulfide) would substantially strengthen the FBEB claims. Also, FTIR experiments appear to be single replicates—error analysis/repeats should be shown.

4. **Stoichiometry and occupancy issues.** The "18%" FdhAB-containing class is derived from 3D classification of flexible particles; classification bias against/for heterogeneous small subunits is well documented, and the true occupancy of Vhu vs FdhAB is uncertain. Please discuss or validate (e.g., MS-based quantification of FdhAB vs Vhu subunits in the preparation). Additionally, the abstract states "over 600 redox cofactors" while the text says 690—reconcile.

5. **Does overexpression artefact the assembly?** HdrB2 is transiently overexpressed; given the 8 MDa size and VhuB-mediated oligomerization, please demonstrate that the endogenous, non-overexpressed assembly has the same stoichiometry (the cryo-ET helps, but the STA is 11 Å and model-docked). A brief quantitative comparison of in situ dimensions vs the SPA map, and discussion of tag positioning effects, would suffice.

6. **Concentration claim of 1.9 µM.** Derived from only 8 tomograms of unspecified lamella quality; given lamellae came from multilayered cells, sampling bias is possible. Please provide per-cell values and clarify whether the values include partially truncated particles at lamella surfaces.

MINOR CONCERNS:

- Abstract: "Cryo-electron tomography further support" — grammar; also "the the Hdr–Vhu–Fwd" typo; "has a modular and adaptable bioenergetic assembly" is awkward.
- Text: "reconstitution" → "reconstruction"; "iron–sufur" typo; "a hourglass" → "an hourglass"; "natural competent" → "naturally competent".
- Extended Data Table 1 is referenced but statistics for the composite/local maps should be clearly itemized, including FSC criteria, map sharpening, and model-to-map fit metrics (Q-scores would be appropriate at these resolutions).
- Clarify how the claimed 4 Å global resolution relates to the local resolutions (3.04–3.41 Å) and map composition (composite map — how generated, and are figures showing composite or single maps?).
- Number of particles in final consensus refinement is given, but per-focused-refinement particle numbers are not; please provide a processing flowchart.
- The claim of ribosome-assisted tomogram refinement is nice; state how many tomograms in total had usable particles (50 of 150?) and why.
- Discussion: statements about ferredoxin allocation to nitrogen fixation are interesting but speculative; soften or cite direct evidence.
- Reference formatting inconsistencies (e.g., "15, 16–17").

DECISION: minor_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript demonstrates that fibrillar adhesions (FBs) anchor the vimentin cytoskeleton to the ECM via plectin 1f, locking the nucleus in a deformed state and setting the timescale of nuclear mechano-response to ~1 hour, effectively acting as a low-pass filter for mechanical stimulation. The authors show that on loss of contractility, YAP and other mechanosensitive factors remain nuclear if FBs are present, but exit if FBs are disrupted, and that this requires vimentin and nesprin3. They further show that FB–vimentin coupling protects the nucleus from deformation and DNA damage under stretch and delays adaptation to soft substrates, supported by multiple experimental approaches and a computational model.

MAJOR CONCERNS: None.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The molecular partner of plectin 1f in FBs is not identified; the discussion speculates on tensin or Hic-5. This is a limitation, but the authors appropriately acknowledge it as a future direction.
- The computational model is simplified and relies on assumptions; however, it is supported by sensitivity analysis and matches experimental trends. The authors should consider explicitly stating that the model is a minimal representation intended to capture qualitative behavior.
- The term "low-pass filter" is used in the abstract and outlook but not formally defined; the authors could briefly explain the concept in the introduction or results for clarity.
- In the photodegradable gel experiments (Fig. 4), the lag time before Sencyt decreases is ~30 min, while the measured FB disassembly time is ~75 min. The authors could clarify how these timescales relate, though the t0.5 of 52 min is consistent.
- Some figure panels are dense, but this is acceptable given the comprehensive nature of the study.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY:
The manuscript by the authors presents the structural and functional characterization of the 8 MDa Hdr–Vhu–Fwd super-assembly from the class I methanogen *Methanococcus maripaludis*. By combining single-particle cryo-EM, in situ cryo-electron tomography, in situ FTIR spectroscopy, and phylogenetic analysis, the authors demonstrate how this massive bioenergetic complex bridges electron bifurcation and CO2 reduction via polyferredoxin subunits (VhuB and FwdF), while also accommodating modular electron-input components (such as FdhAB). This work provides fundamental insights into energy conservation and structural diversification across methanogenic lineages.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
None.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- In the Abstract, there is a duplicated word: "reveals that the the Hdr–Vhu–Fwd super-assembly..." -> please remove the duplicated "the".
- In the "Conformational flexibility and gating" section, there is a small typo: "...distal iron–sufur clusters" should be corrected to "...distal iron–sulfur clusters".
- Please ensure that all accession codes (EMDB IDs, PDB IDs) and source data repositories are fully populated and active upon final production.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY: The paper presents a predictive computational framework for solid-state synthesis that integrates machine-learned transport coefficients for liquid-like interphases into a cellular automaton model (ReactCA). Applied to the Ba–Ti–O system, the model captures the interplay between thermodynamics and diffusion kinetics, and demonstrates that cross-ion correlation effects are essential for accurately predicting phase selectivity. The simulations reproduce key experimental observations across four different precursor ratios and temperature/time profiles.

MAJOR CONCERNS: None.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The comparison with experiments is largely qualitative. Adding quantitative metrics (e.g., phase fraction errors or time-to-formation comparisons) would strengthen the claims of predictive accuracy.
- Several typographical errors are present in the text, e.g., “Ba6Ti27O40” in the Methods section vs “Ba6Ti17O40” in the main text (Reaction 4), and “BaTi2O2” which appears to be a typo for “BaTi2O5”. These should be corrected.
- The assumption of a liquid-like interphase is validated indirectly through agreement with experiments. A more direct justification (e.g., citing experimental evidence for disordered interphases in similar systems) would be helpful, though the current reasoning is plausible.
- The paper would benefit from a brief discussion of the limitations of the approach, particularly regarding systems with variable oxidation states or significant charge transfer, where the current approximations may break down.

DECISION: minor_revision

**SUMMARY:**
The manuscript demonstrates that mitochondrial metabolism, specifically the pyruvate–citrate–acetyl-CoA axis governed by MPC, SLC25A1, and ACLY, acts as a metabolic checkpoint regulating histone acetylation (H3K27ac) and chromatin accessibility at SASP loci. The authors show that this metabolic-epigenetic module functions independently of, but cooperatively with, mtDNA–cGAS–STING inflammatory signaling to drive SASP gene expression. Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of SLC25A1 with CTPI2 in aged mice selectively reduces SASP transcription and chromatin accessibility without altering senescent cell abundance or core systemic metabolism, resulting in marked improvements in neuromuscular performance and healthspan.

**MAJOR CONCERNS:**
- None.

**MINOR CONCERNS:**
- In the Methods section under "ChIP–seq analysis files", there is a slight redundancy in the description of nf-core pipeline parameters and tool descriptions across two adjacent paragraphs. These could be streamlined to avoid repetition.
- Please ensure that all public repository accession numbers for the single-nucleus multiome datasets (snRNA-seq/snATAC-seq) are clearly deposited and referenced in the Data Availability statement upon final production.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY: This manuscript presents a high-throughput all-optical method combining interferometric scattering (iSCAT) and photoluminescence (PL) microscopy to determine the size, emission, and quantum yield of individual CsPbBr3 perovskite nanocrystals in situ. The authors apply this technique to reveal size-dependent PLQY heterogeneity, defect-repair kinetics, and photoinduced degradation dynamics at the single-particle level, providing insights masked by ensemble measurements.

MAJOR CONCERNS: None. The methodology is well-calibrated and validated against TEM and bulk PLQY measurements, and the statistical analyses (covariance, PCA) are appropriate. The key claims—size-dependent PLQY, different enhancement kinetics for different defect types, and power-dependent degradation with Pb0-mediated quenching—are supported by the data and reasonable physical arguments. The authors have adequately addressed the technical challenges of single-particle PLQY determination and provide a compelling demonstration of the method's capabilities.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The abstract sentence "finding material loss decreases at higher laser powers due to the trapping of photoinduced electrons by the formed metallic lead" is slightly convoluted; consider rephrasing for clarity.
- The calibration of iSCAT contrast to volume is performed on a single sample, and the same conversion factor is applied to other samples. The authors should explicitly state whether this conversion is re-validated for each new sample or batch, or discuss the potential impact of batch-to-batch variations in dielectric properties.
- The degradation experiments use the 450-nm laser for both excitation and iSCAT detection, which may introduce absorption-related contrast changes. While SEM confirms size reduction, a brief comment on how the iSCAT signal is disentangled from absorption effects would strengthen the interpretation.
- Some LaTeX formatting artifacts remain in the text (e.g., in the Methods section), which should be cleaned up for final publication.

DECISION: minor_revision

**Review of "Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP" (Round 2)**

SUMMARY: The authors propose that mitochondrial citrate export via SLC25A1 supplies nucleocytosolic acetyl-CoA for histone acetylation at SASP loci, acting as a metabolic–epigenetic arm of SASP regulation that is independent of, but cooperative with, mtDNA–cGAS–STING signalling. Pharmacological inhibition of SLC25A1 with CTPI2 suppresses SASP gene expression and chromatin accessibility in aged mice, improving frailty and muscle function without altering senescent cell burden.

MAJOR CONCERNS:

1. **Pseudoreplication in the single-nucleus multiome experiment (Fig. 7).** The Methods state that quadriceps from 2 groups of 4 mice each were pooled, yielding 2 samples per condition and ~13,400 nuclei total. Analyses in Fig. 7f–k appear to treat nuclei as independent observations (Wilcoxon tests on per-nucleus scores). With n = 2 biological replicates per condition, the statistical support for the key in vivo chromatin conclusions is inadequate. The authors should either (i) provide per-mouse aggregated analyses with appropriate statistics, or ideally (ii) repeat with additional independent mice. At minimum, all claims from this experiment must be qualified and the pooling scheme explicitly disclosed in the figure legends.

2. **Specificity of CTPI2 in vivo.** The central in vivo conclusion rests entirely on a single pharmacological inhibitor. CTPI2 has documented off-target and context-dependent metabolic effects (as the authors themselves note for steatohepatitis). There is no genetic validation in vivo (e.g., SLC25A1 haploinsufficiency or tissue-specific conditional knockout, or an independent SLC25A1 inhibitor/ASO). Given that the entire translational claim hinges on CTPI2, the authors should either provide an orthogonal perturbation in vivo or temper the conclusions considerably.

3. **Partial restoration by acetate (Fig. 1i–k).** Acetate only partially rescues the SASP programme in mitochondria-depleted cells. The manuscript interprets this as consistent with the model, but partial rescue could equally indicate additional mitochondrial contributions (e.g., other acetyl-CoA sources, ROS, signalling). The authors should quantify the fraction of the 51-gene signature restored and discuss alternative interpretations, or test whether higher/alternative acetyl-CoA donors fully rescue.

4. **mtDNA transfection controls (Fig. 5p–q).** The synergy experiment would benefit from key controls: DNase-treated mtDNA, non-CpG or nuclear DNA controls, and confirmation that the transfected mtDNA engages cGAS–STING (e.g., STING dependency of the response, which is implied by Extended Data Fig. 9k but not shown for the reconstitution itself). Without these, the "cooperation" conclusion could reflect nonspecific DNA transfection effects.

5. **Sex-specific effects are not addressed.** The liver RNA-seq shows "more pronounced effects in male mice," and macrophage marker changes only in females, yet the manuscript reports combined-sex analyses for most endpoints and applies two-tailed t-tests pooling sexes. Given known sex dimorphism in both ageing and SASP, the authors should either analyse sex as a factor throughout or justify pooling with evidence of no interaction.

6. **Causality of the human correlation analysis (Extended Data Fig. 13).** Correlations of SLC25A1 expression with a SASP score derived from the authors' own 51-gene signature are circular to some degree (the signature was defined in cultured fibroblasts). The claim that "chronological age alone showed little or no association" is surprising for p16/p21 in GTEx and should be carefully re-examined (tissue composition confounders, RIN covariates).

7. **In vivo epigenetic mechanism.** The in vivo histone acetylation data rely on pan-acetyl-lysine IF in liver (n = 4, single staining run) rather than locus-specific measurements in muscle, where the functional benefit is observed. ChIP or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac at SASP loci from aged muscle would substantially strengthen the claim that the healthspan benefit is mediated through the proposed epigenetic mechanism rather than correlatively.

MINOR CONCERNS:

- Abstract states "improves healthspan in aged mice" — 3 months of treatment in 19–22-month-old mice supports improved function/frailty, but "healthspan" should be used cautiously or defined.
- Fig. 5i uses "uncorrected Fisher's LSD" — please use corrected multiple comparisons.
- Methods contain duplicated, near-identical ChIP-seq processing paragraphs; consolidate.
- Typo: "asset" for "assessed" (grip strength); "2 Kv" inconsistent capitalization; "H2K27ac" should be H3K27ac in Methods.
- Fig. 1c normalization by H3 subtraction is unusual; please clarify why ratio/subtract rather than ratio, and confirm input normalization.
- The 51-gene SASP signature definition and gene list should be provided as a supplementary table.
- CTPI2 dosing (50 mg/kg, 3×/week) — plasma/tissue drug levels or a target-engagement marker in vivo would strengthen interpretation.
- Discussion could acknowledge that SLC25A1 inhibition may affect non-senescent cells; the citrate supplementation data in proliferating cells (Fig. 4b,c) suggest this axis is not senescence-specific.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: This manuscript reports a high-resolution cryo-EM structure of an approximately 8 MDa Hdr–Vhu–Fwd assembly from Methanococcus maripaludis, comprising two Hdr–Vhu rings connected by three tetrameric Fwd modules through VhuB and FwdF polyferredoxins. Cryo-electron tomography is used to visualize similar particles in cells, while classification, spectroscopy and comparative sequence analysis are interpreted as evidence for interchangeable electron-input modules, catalytic coupling and a class-I-specific architecture. The structural work is impressive and potentially important, but several central functional and physiological conclusions remain insufficiently supported.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The infrared experiment does not establish the claimed catalytic coupling from H2 oxidation to CO2 reduction. The 2,338 cm−1 signal is a general CO2 absorption and is not, as written, evidence for “CO2 bound to formate dehydrogenase FdhAB”; moreover, Fwd is presented elsewhere as the CO2-reducing module, whereas FdhAB is proposed as an alternative electron-input module. A decrease in this band alone does not identify formate production and could reflect changes in gas–film partitioning, hydration or baseline response. Direct product quantification, appropriate controls lacking one or both electron acceptors, and clarification of whether Fwd or Fdh is proposed to catalyse the observed reaction are required. Without these data, the manuscript should not state that spectroscopy “corroborated electronic coupling between all catalytic subunits.”
- The in situ experiment was apparently performed with the same plasmid-bearing strain that transiently overexpresses Twin-Strep-tagged HdrB2. Thus, it shows that the assembly can form inside genetically modified, overexpressing cells, but does not by itself demonstrate the endogenous physiological organization or abundance of the native machinery. Overexpression could promote oligomerization or substantially alter the reported 1.9 μM concentration. Tomography of wild-type cells, or cells expressing the tagged subunit from its endogenous locus at native levels, is needed for the strong claims that purification “faithfully reflects the physiological organization” and that the complex forms natively at the measured concentration. The manuscript should also report template-matching false-positive controls, detection thresholds and why concentration was calculated from only eight of the 50 analysed tomograms.
- The proposed Fdh-containing variant requires clearer validation. The text alternately describes FdhAB as replacing Vhu and as binding concurrently with Vhu on opposite sides of an HdrABC dimer. Because classification followed D3 symmetry expansion of a heterogeneous particle population, the authors should demonstrate that the Vhu and Fdh densities coexist within the same physical Hdr dimer rather than arising from separate occupancies or classification/symmetry artefacts. Particle numbers, occupancy distributions, unsymmetrized classifications, map–model validation and evidence distinguishing FdhA2B2 from related proteins should be provided. The assertion that this state represents adaptation to H2 limitation is also unsupported because the cells were grown under H2/CO2 and no environmental perturbation was tested.
- The mechanistic assignment of redox “states” and the Cys–Sec relay is overly strong. The cryo-EM sample does not appear to have been poised at a defined potential, and conformational differences or variability alone do not establish reduced versus oxidized states or electron-transfer gating. Likewise, a continuous cryo-EM density cannot establish a reversible selenenylsulfide relay. Exact cofactor-to-residue distances and map support should be shown, and these sections should either be supported experimentally—for example through redox-dependent structures, spectroscopy or mutagenesis—or explicitly reframed as structural hypotheses rather than mechanistic conclusions.
- The lineage-wide architectural conclusion is not yet adequately supported by the described comparative analysis. Inferring an intact 8 MDa architecture from BLAST hits to two polyferredoxins and selected FwdF cysteines is indirect, and the methods lack a reproducible account of taxon sampling, coverage thresholds, gene-neighbourhood analysis, co-occurrence of all required components and phylogenetic validation. The claim that this architecture is specific to and representative of class I methanogens should be narrowed to the taxa directly supported or strengthened by a systematic analysis. The terminology concerning Methanococcus, Methanobacteria, Methanopyrus, “class I,” Euryarchaeota and TACK should also be made taxonomically consistent.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The architecture and stoichiometry should be described consistently. The assembly contains three tetrameric Fwd complexes/FwdF cores, not a single “tetrameric FwdF core,” and “12 copies of the Hdr–Vhu dimer” is potentially confusing.
- “Continuous, circular electron chain” is misleading unless a closed electron-transfer path is demonstrated. The structure appears to contain repeated branched pathways rather than a catalytic electron circuit around the ring.
- Provide a clear cofactor inventory per protomer and per complete assembly, including the number of tungsten centres versus molybdopterin guanine dinucleotides, and reconcile “over 600” with the stated total of more than 690.
- The manuscript repeatedly conflates structural proximity with demonstrated electron transfer. Statements that the architecture “directly links all active sites,” eliminates reliance on soluble ferredoxin, minimizes diffusional losses or reallocates ferredoxin to nitrogen fixation should be qualified unless supported experimentally.
- The Fdh nomenclature and biochemical directionality need consistent treatment throughout: FdhAB is introduced as an electron-input module but later described as the site of CO2-to-formate conversion.
- Report local-resolution distributions and validation metrics for all deposited focused maps and models, particularly the flexible Vhu and low-occupancy Fdh classes. The model-building description should state how overfitting was assessed.
- The expression procedure is called “transient overexpression,” although cultures were repeatedly passaged under selection; the expression system and relative expression level versus endogenous HdrB2 should be quantified and described accurately.
- Numerous grammatical and typographical issues remain, including “AbstractAbstract,” “the the,” “Cryo-electron tomography further support,” “has a modular,” “species persists,” “a hourglass,” “iron–sufur,” and inconsistent spacing around methyl-H4MPT. The manuscript would benefit from thorough copy-editing.
- Figure 4 and its legend should distinguish gas-phase/dissolved CO2 absorption from enzyme-bound species and should display replicates, quantitative kinetics, uncertainty and independent biological preparations rather than only representative difference spectra.
- The title and abstract should avoid implying universal class-I conservation until the comparative evidence is strengthened.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: The manuscript presents a combined iSCAT–photoluminescence approach intended to determine the size and PLQY of large numbers of individual CsPbBr3 nanocrystals in solution. The authors report size-dependent PLQY, differential responses to post-synthetic passivation, and illumination-induced size loss that is proposed to terminate through metallic-Pb-mediated electron trapping.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
